samples.title: Staff handbook
samples.blurb: Four policies. The switch from leave to expenses happens in the middle of a paragraph.
paragraphs: Every full-time employee receives twenty-five days of paid annual leave, plus public holidays.
Leave is calculated from your start date, so someone who joins in July receives roughly half the allowance in their first year.
Please book time off through the HR portal at least two weeks in advance, and check the team calendar before you do.
Up to five unused days can be carried into the next year; anything beyond that is lost on the first of January.
If you fall ill while on holiday, tell your manager the same day and those days will be recorded as sick leave instead.
Business expenses are repaid through the monthly payroll run once a claim has been approved.
Attach a photo of every receipt to the claim, because card statements alone are not accepted.
Train travel should be booked in standard class unless the journey is longer than four hours.
Claims older than ninety days are refused, so submit them at the end of each trip rather than saving them up.
Your laptop is encrypted, and it must be locked whenever you step away from it, even inside the office.
Passwords need at least fourteen characters, and the password manager provided by IT will generate them for you.
Never install browser extensions that IT has not approved, since several have been caught copying customer data.
If a device is lost or stolen, report it to the IT help desk within one hour so it can be wiped remotely.
Staff may work from home up to three days a week, as agreed with their manager.
The company pays a one-off allowance of £300 toward a desk and chair for your home setup.
Core hours are ten until four, and you should be reachable on chat during that time wherever you are working.

samples.title: Town guide
samples.blurb: Four topics. The section on seasons runs across a paragraph break.
paragraphs: Saltmere grew up around a medieval salt works, and the shallow evaporation pans can still be seen at low tide.
By the 1800s the harbour shipped salt, coal and slate along the coast, and the population tripled in forty years.
The railway arrived in 1872, bringing the first holidaymakers from the industrial towns inland.
Most of the painted terraces on the seafront date from that boom.
Fish is landed every morning at the north quay, and several cafés along the harbour cook whatever came in that day.
The local speciality is smoked mackerel pâté, served on dark rye bread with pickled cucumber.
On Saturdays a farmers' market fills the old salt warehouse with cheese, honey and cider from the surrounding valleys.
Book ahead for dinner in August, when even small restaurants are full by seven.
The town centre is compact, and nearly everything worth seeing is within a twenty-minute walk of the station.
Parking is scarce in summer, so the park-and-ride site on the bypass is the easier option for drivers.
A coastal bus runs every half hour to the neighbouring villages and stops at the start of the cliff path.
Late May and September are the best months to visit, with warm days and far fewer crowds.
July and August bring the regatta and the lantern festival, but prices for rooms can double.
Winter is quiet and many cafés close, though the storms that roll in off the bay draw photographers from all over the country.
Whatever the season, pack a waterproof, because the weather on this stretch of coast changes quickly.

questions.q: When did the railway reach the town?
Where can I buy local cheese?

samples.title: Plant care
samples.blurb: Four topics in three paragraphs. Repotting starts halfway through the paragraph on pests.
paragraphs: Fiddle-leaf figs need a lot of bright, indirect light, ideally from a window that faces east or south.
A plant that sits too far from the glass will drop its lower leaves and grow tall and thin as it reaches for the sun.
Turn the pot a quarter turn every week or two so that all sides get an equal share of light.
Strong afternoon sun through a south-west window can scorch the leaves, leaving brown patches that never recover.
Water only when the top five centimetres of compost feel dry to the touch.
Pour slowly until water runs out of the drainage holes, then empty the saucer after half an hour.
Overwatering is the most common cause of death, because roots sitting in wet soil begin to rot within days.
In winter the plant grows slowly and may need water only once every two or three weeks.
Check the undersides of the leaves each month for spider mites, which leave fine webbing and pale speckles.
Wiping the leaves with a damp cloth removes dust and also dislodges most pests before they spread.
A bad infestation can be treated with insecticidal soap, sprayed every five days for about three weeks.
Repot a young plant every spring into a container no more than five centimetres wider than the old one.
Use a free-draining mix, such as two parts compost to one part bark chips.
Older plants can stay in the same pot for years if you replace the top layer of compost each spring.

How do I spot spider mites?

samples.title: How RAG works
samples.blurb: A plain-language explainer of the setting this project studies. Here topics and paragraphs line up.
paragraphs: A language model only knows what was in its training data, which may be months old and never included your own documents.
Retrieval-augmented generation works around this by looking up relevant passages first and giving them to the model along with the question.
The model then writes its answer from those passages instead of relying on memory alone.
Before anything can be looked up, every document has to be cut into smaller pieces called chunks.
Chunks that are too large bury the useful sentence among unrelated text, and the model may miss it.
Chunks that are too small lose the surrounding context that explains what a sentence refers to.
Cutting where the topic changes, rather than after a fixed number of words, tries to keep each chunk about one thing.
Each chunk is turned into an embedding, a list of numbers that places texts with similar meaning close together.
When a question arrives, it is embedded the same way, and the chunks whose embeddings are closest to it are retrieved.
Only a handful of chunks fit in the prompt, so the ranking decides what the model gets to see.
The retrieved chunks are pasted into the prompt, usually with an instruction to answer only from them.
Because the sources are known, the answer can point back to the exact passage it came from.
If the right chunk was never retrieved, though, the model has nothing to go on and may guess.
That is why the way documents are chunked has a direct effect on whether answers are correct.

questions.q: Why are very large chunks a problem?
What happens if the right chunk is not retrieved?
